content: Prenatal development refers to the intricate process by which an embryo or fetus develops during pregnancy, beginning at fertilization and continuing until birth. This process is often described using terms such as fetal development, embryology, or foetal development. Following fertilization, embryogenesis begins, and by the end of the 10th week of gestational age in humans, the precursors of all major organs are formed. Fertilization When semen is deposited in the vagina, spermatozoa travel through the cervix, uterus, and into the Fallopian tubes. Fertilization typically occurs in the Fallopian tube, where multiple sperm collaborate to penetrate the ovum's protective outer layer. The first sperm to fully penetrate the egg contributes its genetic material (DNA), resulting in the formation of a zygote. The zygote contains the complete genetic information unique to the individual, with half of the nuclear DNA derived from the mother and half from the father. However, mitochondrial DNA is entirely inherited from the mother. Embryonic Period The embryonic period begins at fertilization and lasts until the end of the 10th week of gestation. During this time: The zygote travels down the Fallopian tube, dividing repeatedly to form a morula, a ball of cells. A cavity forms within the morula, creating a blastocyst. The blastocyst reaches the uterus around the fifth day after fertilization. The blastocyst hatches from its glycoprotein shell (zona pellucida) and implants into the uterine lining, a process known as implantation. The inner cell mass of the blastocyst forms the embryo, while the outer layer forms the membranes and placenta. Rapid growth and differentiation occur, leading to the formation of various cell types and the initial development of external features. Changes by Weeks of Gestation Week 2 (Fertilization Week) The zygote undergoes mitotic division (cleavage) without increasing in size. A hollow cavity forms, marking the blastocyst stage. The blastocyst implants into the uterine lining. Week 3 Trophoblast cells proliferate and invade the uterine lining, forming the placenta and embryonic membranes. The yolk sac forms. Embryonic cells flatten into a two-cell-thick disk. The primitive streak and primary stem villi develop. Week 4 The notochord forms in the center of the embryonic disk. A neural groove (future spinal cord) develops, with a brain bulge at one end. The heart tube begins to form and fuse. Somites, the precursors to vertebrae, appear. Week 5 The embryo measures approximately 4 mm and begins to curve into a C-shape. The heart develops further and begins to beat rhythmically. The neural tube closes, and the first signs of the lungs and liver appear. Arm buds and a tail become visible. Week 6 The embryo grows to 8 mm in length. Lens pits and optic cups form, marking the beginning of eye development. Nasal pits and early brain vesicles appear. Limb buds develop into flat paddles, and primitive blood vessels connect to the yolk sac. Week 7 The embryo measures 13 mm in length. The lungs begin to form, and the brain continues to develop. Arms and legs lengthen, with distinguishable hand and foot areas. Digits form, though they may still be webbed. Week 8 The embryo reaches 18 mm in length. Nipple and hair follicle development begins. Elbows and toes become visible, and spontaneous limb movements may be detected via ultrasound. All essential organs have at least begun to form. Fetal Period The fetal period begins at the end of the 10th week of gestation. By this time, the precursors of all major organs are formed. The fetus is less sensitive to environmental exposures than the embryo, though toxic exposures can still cause physiological abnormalities or minor congenital malformations. Weeks 14–17 The fetus grows to about 15 cm in length. Fine hair (lanugo) develops on the head, and the skin becomes nearly transparent. Bones harden, and muscle tissue increases. The fetus begins active movements and makes sucking motions. Week 20 The fetus measures approximately 20 cm in length. Lanugo covers the entire body, and eyebrows, eyelashes, and nails appear. The fetus becomes more active, and the mother may feel movements (quickening). The fetal heartbeat can be heard with a stethoscope. Week 28 The fetus grows to about 38 cm in length and weighs around 1.2 kg. Rapid brain development occurs, and the nervous system begins to control some body functions. The eyelids open and close, and the respiratory system develops to allow gas exchange. A baby born prematurely at this stage may survive with medical intervention. Week 32 The fetus measures 38–43 cm in length and weighs about 2 kg. Body fat increases rapidly, and rhythmic breathing movements occur. Bones are fully developed but remain soft and pliable. Week 36 The fetus reaches 40–48 cm in length and weighs 2.5–3 kg. Lanugo begins to disappear, and body fat continues to increase. Fingernails reach the tips of the fingers. Weeks 37–40 The fetus is considered full-term at 37 weeks. It measures 48–53 cm in length, and lanugo is mostly gone except on the upper arms and shoulders. Fingernails extend beyond the fingertips, and head hair becomes coarser and thicker. This detailed timeline highlights the complex and dynamic process of human prenatal development, emphasizing the critical milestones and vulnerabilities at each stage.
